t: #4031 Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array II — Editorial
o: Given a value range [lower, upper], report maximal contiguous runs of integers in that range absent from nums, as [start, end] pairs in increasing order. Example 1: within [1,12], the present values {3,7,9} split the range into gaps [1,2], [4,6], [8,8], [10,12]. Example 2 shows nums values outside [lower, upper] are irrelevant. With n and the range bounded by 10⁵, both sorting and direct marking are easily fast enough; the output size can be up to ~5·10⁴ ranges.
k: Clamp attention to values inside [lower, upper]; dedupe them and sort.
Missing ranges are exactly the gaps between consecutive covered points, plus the ends of [lower, upper].
Sorting gives O(n log n); a boolean presence array gives O(n + upper) with simpler logic.

a.i: Mark every nums value that lies inside [lower, upper] in a boolean array indexed by value. Then sweep lower..upper, emitting a range whenever the run of unmarked values ends. Very direct and cache-friendly.
s: Allocate present[lower..upper], mark values from nums that fall in range.
Sweep v from lower to upper tracking the start of the current missing run.
When a marked value ends a run, push [start, v−1].
After the sweep, close any trailing run with upper.
a.t: O(n + U) where U = upper − lower + 1 — marking is O(n), the sweep is O(U).

a.n: Approach 2: Sort and Gap Scan (Optimal when range is huge)
a.i: Filter nums to [lower, upper], dedupe, and sort. Walk through the sorted values maintaining `cur` = the smallest not-yet-covered integer; each value greater than cur closes a missing range [cur, v−1]. Finally, if cur ≤ upper, emit [cur, upper]. This uses memory proportional to n rather than the range size.
s: Filter values into [lower, upper], dedupe, sort ascending.
Set cur = lower; for each value v: if v > cur, push [cur, v−1]; set cur = v + 1.
If cur ≤ upper after the loop, push [cur, upper].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting the filtered distinct values dominates; the gap scan is linear.
a.sp: O(n) — the sorted distinct value list.

w: Either approach is interview-ready: pick the boolean array when the value range is comparable to n (as here), and the sort-and-scan when the range could be enormous (e.g., 64-bit bounds) — that's the classic follow-up. Pitfalls: forgetting to clamp nums values outside [lower, upper] (Example 2), duplicates creating spurious empty ranges (dedupe or guard with v > cur), and mishandling the trailing gap after the last present value. Edge cases: no missing integers (Example 3) returns []; lower == upper; nums entirely outside the range returns [[lower, upper]]. Follow-ups: report ranges as strings "a->b" (LeetCode 163 style), or handle ranges too large to enumerate individually.
